A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ALI-CFM research, with matching methods, datasets and core experiments. Their complete main texts and Appendices A–D, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-knot, cell-tracking, single-cell and spatial-transcriptomics experiments, including learned trajectories and numerical EMD results in Tables 1–3.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds MFM evaluations, coupling and marginal-count studies, and numerical regularizer ablations in Tables 4–6.

M1.justification: The interpolant parametrization, adversarial objective, two-stage ALI-CFM procedure and three regularizers remain unchanged. R3GAN training and LAND-based single-cell regularization were already documented in v1 Appendix D.3. Newly evaluated MFM variants are comparators.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same knot distribution, U373 cell-tracking data, EB/Cite/Multi single-cell datasets and breast-cancer tissue sections. The added studies vary marginal counts, couplings, metrics and regularization within this retained coverage.

E2.justification: The central knot comparison replaces time-independent LAND OT-MFM with time-dependent LAND OT-MFM in Figure 2. The cell-tracking comparison additionally evaluates the time-dependent variant while retaining the earlier variant. These substantively revise an important comparator in two principal experiments; comparator membership in Tables 1–3 is unchanged.

E3.justification: The revised knot MFM comparison trains interpolants using intermediate data and uses a 32-unit SELU vector-field network, replacing the earlier end-marginal interpolation setup with a 64-unit ELU vector-field network. Added protocols sweep K from 30 to 1200 and regularizer weights, evaluate interpolant EMD and path energy, and train the additional cell MFM variant for 75,000 epochs with precomputed successive OT maps.

E4.justification: v2 adds marginal-count sensitivity analysis in Figure 8, independent-versus-OT coupling analysis in Figure 9, and time-dependent MFM failure analysis in Figure 11. Appendix D.3.1 adds piecewise-linear and second-derivative regularizer ablations across weights and Cite dimensions. Appendix D.1 also investigates RBF metric-fitting failures and computational cost.

E5.justification: The new Figure 9 loss plot includes a seed=42 label, providing seed information absent from v1. The five-run single-cell reporting and existing ± entries remain unchanged. Tables 4–6 provide point estimates without stated repetition counts, and Figure 9 does not define its shading as a particular uncertainty estimate.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain their numerical values and rankings, but v2 adds substantial numerical and qualitative findings. Tables 4–6 report interpolant EMD, CFM EMD and path energy; for example, Table 4 reports path energy increasing from 300.01 to 87052.14 as the piecewise regularizer weight increases from 0.01 to 10 for the first held-out time. Figure 2 replaces MFM results under changed conditions, and Figures 8, 9 and 11 add further findings.

T1.justification: Section 2.1 explicitly conditions the GAN/Jensen–Shannon equivalence on an optimal discriminator. Appendix B replaces generic coordinate-distribution statements with an explicit isotropic joint Gaussian specification. The two uniqueness theorems and their Appendix A proofs retain their mathematical content apart from numbering.

C1.justification: The main distribution-matching, smoothness, uniqueness and application-performance claims are retained. The Introduction refines the claimed disadvantage of geometry-based approaches toward piecewise interpolation, and Section 5 adds a claim that adversarial training can reduce interpolant-training complexity relative to baselines.

C2.justification: v2 distinguishes failure from time-independent geometry from failure attributed to nonsmooth, time-dependent piecewise interpolation. Appendix D.3.1 adds explanations for why stronger piecewise regularization can increase path energy while stronger second-derivative regularization generally decreases it. The new RBF discussion identifies numerical instability and computational burdens, substantially expanding the mechanism and tradeoff analysis.

D1.justification: Appendices D.1–D.3 add implementation information for the new comparisons, including precomputed OT maps, training budgets, LAND parameters, RBF cluster and epoch choices, and regularizer-weight grids. v2 reports approximately 400 minutes to fit 1199 RBF metric networks on an RTX 3080. It also specifies knot sampling more explicitly; existing code and data access links are retained.

R1.justification: Section 3 revises v1's characterization of MFM as time-independent to acknowledge both time-dependent and time-independent metrics. Section 2.1 explicitly credits existing work for the neural interpolant parametrization. The central distribution-versus-pointwise positioning and cited-work set remain; the Albergo reference update concerns the same work's publication.

P1.justification: v2 copyedits grammar, terminology and citations, revises the abstract's wording, updates the conference header and author information, and expands selected explanations. The main section order and appendix organization remain, with the regularizer study added as subsection D.3.1.

P2.justification: v2 adds multi-panel Figures 8, 9 and 11 and Tables 4–6, and replaces the MFM panels in Figure 2. The earlier tumour-prediction Figure 8 moves into the main text as Figure 6; the raw histology and bifurcation figures are retained as Figures 7 and 10. The author block, link colors and page layout also change.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important weakness in v1's central MFM comparisons by acknowledging and directly evaluating time-dependent MFM on knot and cell data. The added coupling and regularizer studies substantially strengthen evidence for key design choices and expose accuracy/path-energy tradeoffs. Main benchmark scores remain unchanged. Unspecified uncertainty in the new ablations and RBF timings limited to metric fitting constrain some conclusions, but the comparative evidence and diagnostic depth improve substantially.
